system:
You are the analysis agent of a reporting platform for Australia's threatened species. Conservation practitioners — people in government agencies, NGOs and recovery teams who decide where to survey, what to protect and what to escalate — read what you produce. You have read-only SQL access to the platform's database and produce insights from it, each grounded in queries you ran.

# The data

PostgreSQL 17 with PostGIS 3.5. The corpus is every occurrence record the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA) tags as nationally threatened (EPBC Critically Endangered, Endangered or Vulnerable), observed January 2015 to 2026-09-30, from one bulk download (DOI 10.26197/ala.40eee344-07ce-48d2-9ec2-be39574ff4c7): about 2.1 million records, 1,850 taxa, 300+ contributing datasets. Alongside it are all-taxa effort counts per 0.1° cell per month for the same period.

corpus.analysable_occurrences — VIEW — the records to analyse: occurrences that are valid, dated, and not from telemetry (animal-tracking) datasets. Includes population ('wild' or 'managed' — managed means a fenced haven, reintroduction or other managed population, set from the dataset or from corpus.managed_populations) and dataset_kind (the dataset's own kind). Prefer this over occurrences.
  columns: record_id text, source text, source_record_id text, occurrence_id text, harvest_id text, snapshot_page text, fetched_at timestamp with time zone, data_resource_uid text, license text, taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, national_status text, event_date timestamp with time zone, first_loaded_at timestamp with time zone, decimal_latitude double precision, decimal_longitude double precision, coordinate_uncertainty_m double precision, state_province text, ibra_region text, locality text, geom USER-DEFINED, basis_of_record text, individual_count integer, recorded_by_pseudonym text, occurrence_remarks text, event_remarks text, source_assertions ARRAY, is_valid boolean, issue_count integer, cell_lat numeric, cell_lon numeric, event_day date, managed_by_rule boolean, dataset_kind text, population text

corpus.datasets — TABLE — contributing datasets; kind is 'wild', 'managed' (fenced havens, reintroductions) or 'telemetry' (excluded from analysable_occurrences).
  columns: data_resource_uid text, name text, kind text, kind_reason text, first_seen_at timestamp with time zone

corpus.effort_cells — TABLE — ALL-taxa record counts (threatened or not, telemetry excluded) per 0.1° cell per month: the denominator for reporting rates. Join on cell_lat/cell_lon and month.
  columns: cell_lat numeric, cell_lon numeric, period_start date, period_end date, records integer, harvest_id text

corpus.harvest_runs — TABLE — provenance of each harvest (the corpus download and the effort counts).
  columns: harvest_id text, harvest_key text, run_id text, source text, description text, query jsonb, started_at timestamp with time zone, finished_at timestamp with time zone, expected_records integer, retrieved_records integer, complete boolean, corpus_hash text, request_count integer, warnings jsonb, analysis jsonb, loaded_at timestamp with time zone

corpus.managed_populations — TABLE — curated rules marking managed populations: a taxon in a state (optionally narrowed to an IBRA region and a dataset), e.g. Bilby in NSW, where it survives only in fenced havens, or Woylie in AWC's Mt Gibson haven. Already applied in analysable_occurrences.population.
  columns: taxon_concept_id text, state_province text, note text, rule_id integer, ibra_region text, data_resource_uid text

corpus.occurrences — TABLE — every canonical occurrence record, telemetry included. event_date is the observation instant (timestamptz); event_day is its Australian Eastern local date. geom is a PostGIS Point (SRID 4326); cell_lat/cell_lon are the 0.1° grid cell (rounded to nearest, as ALA assigns them).
  columns: record_id text, source text, source_record_id text, occurrence_id text, harvest_id text, snapshot_page text, fetched_at timestamp with time zone, data_resource_uid text, license text, taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, national_status text, event_date timestamp with time zone, first_loaded_at timestamp with time zone, decimal_latitude double precision, decimal_longitude double precision, coordinate_uncertainty_m double precision, state_province text, ibra_region text, locality text, geom USER-DEFINED, basis_of_record text, individual_count integer, recorded_by_pseudonym text, occurrence_remarks text, event_remarks text, source_assertions ARRAY, is_valid boolean, issue_count integer, cell_lat numeric, cell_lon numeric, event_day date, managed_by_rule boolean

corpus.taxa — TABLE — one row per taxon (key taxon_concept_id); national_status is the EPBC status ALA attached.
  columns: taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, taxon_rank text, kingdom text, phylum text, taxon_class text, taxon_order text, family text, genus text, national_status text, status_seen_at timestamp with time zone

corpus.taxon_tiers — VIEW — per taxon: analysable records since 2015, last_record_day, and statistical_tier (≥100 records since 2015).
  columns: taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, national_status text, records_since_2015 bigint, last_record_day date, statistical_tier boolean

Useful facts: EPSG:3577 (Australian Albers, equal-area, metres) is available for gridding and areas; ibra_region is the IBRA 7 bioregion (null offshore — IBRA covers land only); coordinate_uncertainty_m is the radius the true position may lie within.

**Dates: use event_day** (the Australian Eastern local date) for every date window, count by period and date you report — not event_date, which is an instant stored in UTC and would put early-morning Australian records on the previous day.

# Known properties of this data — read before interpreting anything

- **Records measure effort as much as animals.** These are mostly opportunistic records. All-taxa recording roughly doubled between 2017–19 and 2022–24 (about 1.9×), so counts and range measures grow with effort. Use corpus.effort_cells as a denominator where it matters.
- **Recent months are incomplete.** Datasets reach ALA months to a year late: January–August 2026 holds about 20% of the records January–August 2024 holds, and eBird (the largest dataset) has not loaded 2026 at all. A recent decline is not evidence of anything until this is accounted for.
- **Sources start and stop.** A compilation that ends in 2020, or a targeted survey wound up inside an ongoing state atlas, looks exactly like range loss. Check which datasets carry a taxon's records in each period before calling a change real.
- **Locations vary in precision.** About half the analysable records are located to within 2 km; about a third state no uncertainty; ALA generalises many sensitive species to roughly 10 km.
- **Managed populations** (population = 'managed': fenced havens, reintroductions) are in the analysable view and are not wild trend.
- **National status** is as ALA attached it. Never infer, change or second-guess a taxon's conservation status.
- Taxonomy can shift: a taxon "disappearing" from a region can be a name re-assignment.

# How to work

- Call run_sql with one SELECT (or WITH … SELECT) per call, no trailing statements. Results are capped at 200 rows and queries time out after 30 s, so aggregate in SQL rather than pulling rows. Each call returns a query_id.
- Record each insight with record_insight as soon as it is established. Every insight cites the query_ids whose results support it, and every number in it must be a value those queries returned or simple arithmetic on them. Do not state figures you did not query.
- taxon_concept_id must be copied exactly from corpus.taxa; when an insight is about several taxa, put the main one there (or null) and list the others in related_taxa; region is an IBRA region name exactly as in ibra_region, or null for a national insight; period_start and period_end are the window the insight describes.
- Say how confident you are and why, in the confidence field: record counts, the datasets involved, effort, precision, and any artefact that could explain the pattern.
- When you have recorded everything worth recording, stop.

tools.description: Run one read-only SQL query (a single SELECT or WITH … SELECT) against the corpus. Returns a query_id, the columns and up to 200 rows. Cite the query_id in any insight that relies on the result.

sql.description: One SELECT or WITH … SELECT statement.

purpose.description: One line: what this query is for.

tools.name: record_insight
tools.description: Record one insight. Every figure must come from the cited queries.

taxon_concept_id.description: Exactly as in corpus.taxa, or null for a non-taxon insight.

related_taxa.description: Optional: other taxon_concept_ids this insight is about, exactly as in corpus.taxa.

region.description: IBRA region name exactly as in ibra_region, or null for national.

period_start.description: YYYY-MM-DD — start of the window the insight describes.

figures.description: The numbers behind the insight, as returned by your queries.

confidence.description: Why this should or should not be trusted: records, datasets, effort, precision, possible artefacts.

summary.description: One or two sentences a practitioner can act on.

query_ids.description: The run_sql query_ids whose results support this insight.

messages.content:
Report month: 2026-09 (2026-09-01 to 2026-09-30). Compute the three insights below exactly as defined and record them with record_insight, using the insight_type given. "Analysable" means corpus.analysable_occurrences. The statistical tier is taxa with statistical_tier = true in corpus.taxon_tiers.

## 1. silent_species — period 2023-10-01 to 2026-09-30
(a) Silent: taxa in corpus.taxa with no analysable record in that window (whatever their record count).
(b) Evidence gap: taxa with fewer than 10 analysable records since 2015.
(c) Regional silence: a taxon and IBRA region where the taxon had at least 5 analysable records in 2015–2019 but none in the window, while the taxon was still recorded nationally in the window.
Record one headline insight per kind (taxon and region null; figures {kind: "silent" | "evidence_gap" | "regional_silence", count}), then individual insights for the most important cases, up to 15 per kind (figures {kind, last_record_date, records_since_2015, …}, last_record_date as event_day; regional ones with region set).

## 2. range_change — statistical tier, 2017–2019 against 2022–2024 (period 2022-01-01 to 2024-12-31)
Per taxon and window, from analysable records with coordinates:
Wild records only (population = 'wild').
- AOO 10 km: distinct 10 km cells on an EPSG:3577 grid, all records; area = cells × 100 km².
- AOO 2 km: distinct 2 km cells, only records with coordinate_uncertainty_m ≤ 2000; area = cells × 4 km².
- EOO: area of the convex hull of all records, km².
Flag "contraction" or "expansion" when the 10 km AOO changes by at least 30% and both windows have at least 20 records.
Record headline insights with the count of contractions and of expansions (figures {flag, count}), then individual insights for the most important flagged taxa, up to 15 (figures {flag, aoo_10km_km2: {baseline, recent, change}, aoo_2km_km2: {baseline, recent, change}, eoo_km2: {baseline, recent, change}, records: {baseline, recent}}, change as a fraction).

## 3. notable_record — records in 2026-09 of statistical-tier taxa
A record is notable if it is more than 100 km from every earlier analysable record of the taxon (since 2015), or in an IBRA region with no earlier record of the taxon, or in a calendar month holding less than 1% of the taxon's 2015–2019 records (judged only where the taxon has at least 100 such records). Group by taxon and IBRA region: one insight per group, up to 30 (figures {reasons: [...], records, max_distance_to_prior_km}, reasons drawn from "outside_range", "new_region", "out_of_season").

Beyond these, record anything else a practitioner should know as insight_type "other".

input.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM corpus.taxa) taxa, (SELECT count(*) FROM corpus.taxon_tiers) tiers, (SELECT count(*) FROM corpus.taxon_tiers WHERE statistical_tier) stat, (SELECT count(*) FROM corpus.taxon_tiers WHERE records_since_2015<10) gap, (SELECT min(event_day)::text||' '||max(event_day)::text FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences) span, (SELECT count(*) FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences) n
input.purpose: Basic corpus sizes

input.sql:
WITH w AS (SELECT DISTINCT taxon_concept_id FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences WHERE event_day BETWEEN '2023-10-01' AND '2026-09-30')
SELECT count(*) silent,
 count(*) FILTER (WHERE tt.records_since_2015=0) zero_records,
 count(*) FILTER (WHERE tt.statistical_tier) silent_stat,
 count(*) FILTER (WHERE tt.records_since_2015>=10) silent_ge10
FROM corpus.taxa t JOIN corpus.taxon_tiers tt USING (taxon_concept_id)
WHERE t.taxon_concept_id NOT IN (SELECT taxon_concept_id FROM w)
input.purpose: Count silent taxa (no analysable record 2023-10-01..2026-09-30)

input.sql:
SELECT count(*) gap, count(*) FILTER (WHERE records_since_2015=0) zero, count(*) FILTER (WHERE records_since_2015 BETWEEN 1 AND 4) one_to_four, count(*) FILTER (WHERE records_since_2015 BETWEEN 5 AND 9) five_to_nine,
 count(*) FILTER (WHERE national_status ILIKE '%critical%') cr
FROM corpus.taxon_tiers WHERE records_since_2015<10
input.purpose: Evidence gap taxa breakdown

input.sql: SELECT national_status, count(*) FROM corpus.taxa GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC
input.purpose: Status values

content.text: Now the most important silent taxa: those with the most records since 2015.

input.sql:
WITH w AS (SELECT DISTINCT taxon_concept_id FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences WHERE event_day BETWEEN '2023-10-01' AND '2026-09-30'),
s AS (SELECT tt.* , t.taxon_class FROM corpus.taxon_tiers tt JOIN corpus.taxa t USING (taxon_concept_id) WHERE taxon_concept_id NOT IN (SELECT taxon_concept_id FROM w)),
d AS (SELECT a.taxon_concept_id, count(DISTINCT a.data_resource_uid) nds, string_agg(DISTINCT d.name, ' | ') dsn, count(*) FILTER (WHERE population='managed') managed, max(event_day) FILTER (WHERE population='wild') last_wild
 FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences a JOIN corpus.datasets d USING (data_resource_uid) WHERE a.taxon_concept_id IN (SELECT taxon_concept_id FROM s) GROUP BY 1)
SELECT s.taxon_concept_id, s.scientific_name, s.vernacular_name, s.national_status, s.taxon_class, s.records_since_2015, s.last_record_day, d.nds, d.managed, d.last_wild, left(d.dsn,200) dsn
FROM s JOIN d USING (taxon_concept_id) ORDER BY s.records_since_2015 DESC LIMIT 40
input.purpose: Silent taxa ranked by record count since 2015, with datasets

content.text: Now record headline silent and evidence-gap insights.

confidence.notes: The count is exact: taxa in corpus.taxa with no analysable record dated 2023-10-01 to 2026-09-30. Every taxon has at least one record since 2015. Of the 376, 313 have fewer than 10 records since 2015, so most of this silence comes from sparse recording, not lost populations. Silence is also inflated by data lag (2026 is far from complete, and eBird has no 2026 data) and by sources that stopped: Fauna Atlas N.T. has 1 record after 2023 and the NESP A12 compilation ends in 2020 (query 161). Treat silence as 'unconfirmed', not 'absent'.

input.summary: 376 of 1,852 EPBC-listed taxa (20%) have no analysable record in the last three years (Oct 2023 to Sep 2026). 10 of them are statistical-tier taxa and 63 have at least 10 records since 2015. These 63 are the priority list for checking whether the silence comes from no survey work, delayed data delivery or a real loss.

confidence.notes: Exact count from corpus.taxon_tiers (records_since_2015 < 10, analysable records). Fewer than 10 records can mean a genuinely rare taxon, generalised or withheld sensitive records, or data not shared with ALA. It does not show that the population is small.

input.summary: 635 listed taxa (34% of 1,852) have fewer than 10 analysable records since 2015, including 178 Critically Endangered taxa. For these taxa, ALA data cannot support any trend or range assessment, so targeted surveys or data-sharing agreements are needed.

confidence.notes: All 2,935 records come from Fauna Atlas N.T. That atlas fell from 4,447 records in 2018 to 133 in 2023 and 1 in 2024, so the silence almost certainly reflects the source drying up, not the animal (query 163). It is also an NT-only subspecies of a declining northern mammal, so a genuine decline cannot be ruled out.

input.summary: The Black-footed Tree-rat (NT subspecies, Djintamoonga) is the largest silent taxon: 2,935 records since 2015, but none since 28 Oct 2020. Every record came from Fauna Atlas N.T., which has almost stopped supplying ALA. Ask NT DEPWS for post-2020 survey data before reading this as a decline.

confidence.notes: Records come from Flora Atlas N.T. and the NT Herbarium. Flora Atlas N.T. peaked at 10,529 records in 2022 and fell to 28 in 2025 (query 163), so the silence partly reflects reduced supply. Typhonium mirabile is a wet-season ephemeral geophyte, so it is detectable for only a few months a year. Its congener T. praetermissum still has 3,986 records in the window (query 169), so NT Typhonium surveys did continue to 2024 and later.

input.summary: Typhonium mirabile (EN, NT) had 920 records, mostly a 2020–22 survey pulse, then none after 1 Apr 2022, even though surveys of the related T. praetermissum continued. Check whether the 2023–24 wet-season NT surveys looked for it.

confidence.notes: Records come from NSW BioNet Atlas and the NSW AVH feed. BioNet is still delivering (176,020 records in the window, latest 2026-09-20; query 161), so this is not a source stopping. The likely cause is a targeted survey ending rather than plant loss, because a long-lived conifer is unlikely to vanish in three years.

input.summary: Callitris oblonga subsp. parva (CR, NSW) had 788 BioNet records but none since 20 Sep 2022, even though BioNet is still delivering. Confirm with NSW Saving our Species whether monitoring stopped or results simply have not been uploaded.

confidence.notes: All records come from two NESP research compilations: NESP A12, which ends in 2020 (query 161), and the NESP euryhaline elasmobranch fishing database (2011–2019). The silence is a source ending. Its congener Glyphis glyphis has only 1 record in the window (query 169), which shows that northern river sharks have generally gone unrecorded since those projects closed.

input.summary: The Northern River Shark (Glyphis garricki, EN) has had no record since 1 Dec 2019. All 650 records came from NESP projects that ended. A data-sharing request to current northern Australia elasmobranch monitoring programs is needed, because ALA has no current evidence on this species.

confidence.notes: Records come from Flora Atlas N.T. and the NT Herbarium. Flora Atlas supply fell sharply after 2024 (query 163), but this taxon has been silent since early 2021, well before that drop. It is an ephemeral wet-season geophyte.

input.summary: Typhonium jonesii (EN, NT) has had no record since 21 Feb 2021, which is more than 5 wet seasons, despite 631 records in 2015–21. It is a priority for a wet-season presence check at known sites.

confidence.notes: Records come from Fauna Atlas N.T. and the NT Museum (OZCAM). Fauna Atlas N.T. was still delivering about 3,000–4,400 records a year in 2017–2019 and several hundred a year in 2020–2022 (query 163), yet this taxon was silent throughout. That makes the gap more meaningful than for the mainland subspecies.

input.summary: The Melville Island Black-footed Tree-rat (VU) has had no record since 7 Nov 2018, despite 254 records in 2015–18. The gap began while the NT atlas was still active. Tiwi Islands monitoring data should be sought urgently.

confidence.notes: This is a single-source taxon (Fauna Atlas N.T.). Its last record is from 2017, when that atlas was at full output (query 163). A survey that ended is still the most likely explanation.

input.summary: The Carpentarian Rock-rat (EN, NT Gulf country) has had no record for over 9 years (last 23 Jul 2017), despite 163 records in 2015–17. A status check with the NT is warranted.

confidence.notes: Records come from four sources (iNaturalist, WOLL herbarium, NSW AVH, BioNet), all still active. It is a short-lived, fire-responsive herb, so a post-fire flush followed by absence is plausible.

input.summary: Illawarra Irene (Irenepharsus trypherus, EN, NSW) has had no record since 21 Jan 2022, after 134 records from four sources. It is a short-lived herb whose occurrence fluctuates, so a check of known Illawarra escarpment sites is warranted.

confidence.notes: All 133 records fall in 2020–2022 (BioNet and iNaturalist). This looks like a single survey pulse, probably post-fire, rather than ongoing monitoring that later stopped finding it.

input.summary: Cyphanthera scabrella (EN, NSW) was recorded only in a 2020–22 pulse of 133 records, with none since 25 Jan 2022. Check whether any follow-up survey was carried out.

confidence.notes: The last record falls just before the window starts, and the taxon has seven contributing sources. Its recent silence is probably an artefact of lag and chance.

input.summary: Pokolbin Mallee (Eucalyptus pumila, VU, Hunter Valley) is only marginally silent: its last record is 13 Sep 2023, just before the window. Recording fell from 108 records in 2015–19 to 23 in 2020–23. This is low priority, but worth an opportunistic check.

confidence.notes: All records come from time-limited research datasets (a 2017–18 eDNA survey and NESP compilations ending 2019–2020). Other sawfish (Pristis pristis, P. zijsron) are still recorded in the window (query 169), so sawfish recording continues, but not for this species.

confidence.notes: Four sources, all still active. Most records come from a 2020–23 pulse.

input.summary: Dwarf Heath Casuarina (Allocasuarina defungens, EN, NSW north coast) has had no record since 9 Jan 2023, after 62 records in 2020–23. Check whether monitoring continued.

confidence.notes: Single source (NSW BioNet). The records are a 2020–23 survey pulse, so the silence is most likely the survey ending.

content.text:
I've recorded all three insight sets plus five "other" insights (85 in total). The main finding is that in this report most apparent losses, contractions and silences come from data sources that have stopped or slowed, not from evidence about the animals or plants. The NT and Victorian state atlases, and a set of NESP research projects that have ended, account for most of them.

Two of my recorded insights contained errors, and I recorded corrections; please read them together:
- **Lenwebbia sp. Main Range:** I wrote that most records came from the Myrtle Rust Surveys. In fact 36 of its 56 records are NSW BioNet (none after June 2019); a separate "other" insight sets this right.
- **Freshwater Sawfish (Darwin Coastal):** I said the two NESP datasets roughly halve its baseline through duplication. A direct check shows 74 of 78 records in one dataset recur in the other, so that is about right for sawfish. Across the whole dataset, though, only 78 of 516 records match exactly. The duplication insight records this.

I also merged the Bilby's Murchison record into its Gascoyne insight, then recorded Murchison separately as well, so it appears twice.

**1. Silent species (Oct 2023 – Sep 2026)**
- **Silent:** 376 of 1,852 taxa have no record in the window. 10 of them are statistical-tier taxa and 63 have at least 10 records since 2015.
- **Evidence gap:** 635 taxa have fewer than 10 records since 2015, including 178 Critically Endangered.
- **Regional silence:** 184 taxon–region pairs (130 taxa, 65 regions).
- **Individual cases:** 15 silent taxa and 15 regional pairs. The silent taxa include both NT Black-footed Tree-rat subspecies, the Carpentarian Rock-rat, Northern River Shark, Dwarf Sawfish and Callitris oblonga subsp. parva. The more credible regional silences are those where recording effort held up or rose: Regent Honeyeater in the New England Tablelands, Swift Parrot in Nandewar, Black-tailed Godwit in the Riverina, Smoky Mouse in the South East Corner, and Western Kermadec Petrel on Lord Howe.
- **Probable data errors:**
  - The Southern Bent-winged Bat records in the Sydney Basin are very likely a subspecies misassignment.
  - The mainland NSW "Pacific Robin" records are probably Scarlet Robins under an old name.

**2. Range change (2017–19 vs 2022–24)**
- 409 taxa qualified; 35 show a contraction and 228 an expansion.
- The expansions mostly reflect recording effort roughly doubling over the period, not range growth.
- Most of the largest contractions are explained by a baseline source stopping: Olive Ridley Turtle, the two coastal dolphins, Arnhem Brushtail Possum, White Shark and Bar-tailed Godwit.
- The most credible contraction is the Regent Honeyeater: records held steady (1,352 vs 1,203) but its 10 km area of occupancy halved, and it has nearly vanished from SE Queensland and north-east Victoria. Needle Wattle and Turnip Copperburr show smaller-scale contractions that need a repeat survey to confirm.

**3. Notable records (September 2026)**
- 41 taxon–region groups qualified; I recorded 30.
- Every one is an unvetted iNaturalist observation, and several are clearly misidentifications or garden plants. The clearest error is a Brush-tailed Tree-rat in Victoria, 2,742 km outside its range. The planted ones are Macadamia on the tablelands and Magenta Lilly Pilly in south-west WA.
- Worth verifying: Bilby in the Gascoyne and Murchison, Mertens' Water Monitor in the Mitchell Grass Downs, Northern Blue-tongued Skink near Mount Isa, and Spectacled Flying-fox inland in the Einasleigh Uplands.
- Treat this month's records as leads, not confirmed occurrences.

**Other**
- NT data have nearly stopped reaching ALA: the NT fauna atlas has 1 record since Oct 2023.
- Victorian atlas threatened-species records roughly halved between the two range windows while national recording doubled.
- 89% of September 2026 records come from iNaturalist, because other sources lag by months.

The single most useful action is to ask the NT and Victorian governments for their missing survey data. Many of the silences and contractions above can't be judged until that arrives.
